docs.title: Design Guides
docs.text: Design guides cover design decisions, platform behavior, and architectural considerations for working with Business Events. Unlike scenarios, which walk through a complete solution end to end, design guides focus on a single concept you can apply across any project.

docs.title: Event-Driven Architectures in Microsoft Fabric
docs.text:
Scheduled checks and direct calls work well when timing and dependencies are explicit. They become less suitable when several teams need to react independently to the same finding, or when work should start after a specific change rather than another scheduled check.

Event-driven architecture separates the fact from the response. A workload or service emits an event describing what happened. Subscribed workloads apply their own policies and start the relevant action, without the source having to call each recipient.

docs.title: Why it matters for Fabric
docs.text:
In Microsoft Fabric, this can mean bringing a store sales exception to operations, flagging a failed revenue refresh for finance support, or loading a supplier manifest after its arrival in Azure storage.

Each design needs an identifiable source, an event with a clear meaning, a policy that selects the relevant cases, and a concrete response. The event family depends on what happened: a business finding, a Fabric platform change, or a change in an Azure resource.

docs.title: Business Events: investigate a store sales drop
docs.text:
Store operations needs to know which locations have a significant transaction-volume drop, with enough context to begin an investigation. A Notebook compares actual and expected hourly transactions and shares each store finding as a Business Event. Activator owns the response policy: notify operations only when the deviation is strictly below -30%.

flowchart TB
    S[("<b>Source Eventhouse</b><br/>Expected and actual<br/>transactions by store")]
    NB["<b>Notebook</b><br/>Compares hourly<br/>store sales"]
    BE(["<b>Business Event</b><br/>Store sales finding"])
    ACT["<b>Activator</b><br/>Selects deviations<br/>below -30%"]
    T["<b>Teams</b><br/>Operations receives<br/>the investigation context"]
    H[("<b>Eventhouse</b><br/>Store finding history")]

    S -->|"Hourly sales"| NB
    NB -->|"Store finding"| BE
    BE -->|"Deviation"| ACT
    ACT -->|"Sales exception"| T
    BE -.->|"Optional history"| H

The business contract is Retail.Sales.VolumeAlert, not "the Notebook finished." The finding can support another response without changing the sales comparison. Optional Analyze in Eventhouse, selected when creating the Business Event, records finding history separately from the required source Eventhouse.

The outcome is an investigation prompt, not a diagnosis or evidence that sales recovered. The Sales Volume Alert Workbook implements this pattern.

docs.title: Fabric Events: flag a failed revenue refresh
docs.text:
Finance support needs to know when the daily revenue-data refresh fails, so a failed load is not mistaken for current reporting. Fabric Events expose the job lifecycle automatically; the pipeline does not need additional code to describe its own failure.

flowchart TB
    P["<b>Data Pipeline</b><br/>Runs the daily<br/>revenue-data refresh"]
    FE(["<b>Fabric job event</b><br/>Revenue refresh failure"])
    ACT["<b>Activator</b><br/>Matches the monitored<br/>revenue pipeline"]
    T["<b>Teams</b><br/>Finance support receives<br/>the failed run context"]

    P -->|"Failed refresh"| FE
    FE -->|"Job identifiers"| ACT
    ACT -->|"Failed run context"| T

Select Microsoft.Fabric.ItemJobFailed and scope the Activator rule to the intended data.workspaceId and data.itemId. Include data.jobStatus and data.jobInstanceId in the notification so support can identify the run and its outcome; this event type also covers stuck or canceled jobs. The platform event does not explain the cause, validate the report, or retry the load.

See the Fabric job event types and payload. The event source and its Activator item must be in the same region.

docs.title: Azure Events: load a supplier delivery manifest
docs.text:
Receiving needs the supplier's delivery manifest available for planning without repeatedly checking a storage folder. Azure Events provide the file-arrival signal from Azure Blob Storage. A matching arrival starts a configured ingestion pipeline rather than a notification that someone still needs to turn into a load.

flowchart TB
    SA[("<b>Azure Blob Storage</b><br/>Supplier delivery<br/>manifest files")]
    AE(["<b>Azure event</b><br/>Manifest file created<br/>or replaced"])
    ACT["<b>Activator</b><br/>Selects arrivals in the<br/>manifests container"]
    P["<b>Data Pipeline</b><br/>Reads and validates<br/>the referenced file"]
    L[("<b>Lakehouse</b><br/>Delivery manifest rows<br/>for receiving plans")]

    SA -->|"File available"| AE
    AE -->|"Blob URL"| ACT
    ACT -->|"Manifest URL"| P
    P -->|"Validated rows"| L

The Azure Blob Storage event source connects the storage account to Fabric. Activator can act on its unstreamed events; conversion to an Eventstream data stream is not required for this route. Filter Microsoft.Storage.BlobCreated to the manifests container and pass data.url to a pipeline parameter.

The event contains metadata, not the manifest rows. The pipeline reads the file through its configured storage connection, validates it and writes the Lakehouse. Its load logic must handle repeated notifications and file replacements. A stored manifest does not confirm that the physical delivery arrived.

docs.title: Handling Retries
docs.text:
Business Events includes built-in retry behavior. If delivery does not succeed on the first attempt, the platform automatically retries for up to 24 hours. After that window, the event is no longer retried.

This means retry handling is fully managed — you do not need to implement retry logic in your publisher or consumer.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    P["<b>Publisher</b>"]
    BE["<b>Business Event</b><br/>'Retail.Inventory.LowStockThreshold'"]
    C["<b>Consumer</b>"]
    X["<b>Event expired</b>"]

    P -->|"Publishes event"| BE
    BE -->|"Delivery attempt"| C
    C -->|"Delivery fails"| BE
    BE -->|"Retries automatically<br/>for up to 24 hours"| C
    BE -->|"After 24 hours<br/>no more retries"| X

docs.title: What this means for publishers
docs.text:
Your publish call succeeds as soon as the platform accepts the event. You do not need to:

  • Implement exponential backoff
  • Track delivery status
  • Re-publish on failure
# This is all you need — no retry wrapper required
notebookutils.businessEvents.publish(
    workspace, schema_set, event_type, event_data, dataVersion='v1'
)

docs.title: What this means for consumers
docs.text: Consumers should be idempotent — designed to handle receiving the same event more than once without side effects. Because the platform retries on delivery failure, a consumer that partially processed an event and then failed may receive it again.

docs.title: Making consumers idempotent
docs.text:
Use the CloudEvents id field (available in the envelope) as a deduplication key:

// In Eventhouse — check if event was already processed
['Retail.Inventory.LowStockThreshold']
| where id == "a8f3c1d2-..."
| count

For Activator, idempotency is handled naturally — the alert condition evaluates each event independently.

docs.title: Retry window considerations
docs.text: Scenario Recommendation Event represents a time-sensitive signal (e.g., fraud alert) Design consumers to process quickly; stale delivery within 24h may still be actionable Event drives a one-time action (e.g., send email) Make the action idempotent or check for duplicates before acting Consumer is temporarily unavailable Events will be retried — no publisher changes needed

docs.title: Multi-Consumer Fanout
docs.text: Fanout is a pattern where a single Business Event is consumed by multiple independent consumers simultaneously. Because Business Events is a pub/sub system, publishers do not need to know how many consumers exist — each consumer subscribes independently.

docs.title: One event, many consumers
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    P["<b>Publisher</b><br/>Notebook / UDF / Eventstream"]
    BE["<b>Business Event</b><br/>'Retail.Sales.VolumeAlert'"]
    A["<b>Activator</b><br/>Send Teams alert"]
    B["<b>Eventhouse</b><br/>Store for analytics"]
    C["<b>Activator</b><br/>Trigger reorder pipeline"]

    P -->|"publish"| BE
    BE -->|"consume"| A
    BE -->|"consume"| B
    BE -->|"consume"| C

Each consumer subscribes independently. Adding a new consumer does not require any change to the publisher.

docs.title: Alert + analytics
docs.text:
The most common combination — one consumer reacts in real time, another stores for historical analysis.

flowchart TB
    P["<b>Publisher</b>"]
    BE["<b>Business Event</b><br/>'Retail.Sales.VolumeAlert'"]
    ACT["<b>Activator</b><br/>Real-time alert"]
    EH["<b>Eventhouse</b><br/>Historical analytics"]

    P -->|"publish"| BE
    BE -->|"consume"| ACT
    BE -->|"consume"| EH

When to use: Any event where you need both immediate action and long-term visibility.

docs.title: Alert + automation
docs.text:
Two Activator consumers with different actions — one notifies a human, another triggers an automated workflow.

flowchart TB
    P["<b>Publisher</b>"]
    BE["<b>Business Event</b><br/>'Retail.Sales.VolumeAlert'"]
    A1["<b>Activator Rule 1</b><br/>Send email notification"]
    A2["<b>Activator Rule 2</b><br/>Trigger Power Automate flow"]

    P -->|"publish"| BE
    BE -->|"consume"| A1
    BE -->|"consume"| A2

When to use: When a signal requires both human awareness and an automated response, and you want to manage them independently.

docs.title: Cross-domain fanout
docs.text:
A single business signal consumed by teams in different domains, each with their own logic.

flowchart TB
    P["<b>Publisher</b><br/>Retail workload"]
    BE["<b>Business Event</b><br/>'Retail.Customer.MilestoneReached'"]
    A["<b>Marketing team</b><br/>Activator → loyalty email"]
    B["<b>Analytics team</b><br/>Eventhouse → cohort analysis"]
    C["<b>Finance team</b><br/>Activator → discount approval"]

    P -->|"publish"| BE
    BE -->|"consume"| A
    BE -->|"consume"| B
    BE -->|"consume"| C

When to use: When a business signal has value across multiple teams or domains, and each team should own their consumer independently.

docs.title: How to set up fanout
docs.text:
Each consumer is created independently — there is no fanout configuration on the publisher side.

Consumer How to add Activator Real-Time Hub → Business events → Set alert → configure new rule Eventhouse Enabled at Business Event creation time via the "Analyze in Eventhouse" checkbox

To add a second Activator consumer, simply create a new alert rule on the same Business Event. The two rules run independently and do not interfere with each other.

docs.title: Design considerations
docs.text:
Keep consumers independent. Each consumer should be able to fail, restart, or be updated without affecting others.

Do not use fanout to sequence work. If Consumer B must run after Consumer A completes, fanout is not the right pattern — use a dedicated orchestration mechanism instead.

Monitor each consumer separately. A delivery failure to one consumer does not affect delivery to others. Track consumer health individually.

docs.title: Schema Versioning
docs.text: Business Event schemas can evolve over time. This pattern covers how to update a schema and what changes are required on both the publisher and consumer side.

docs.title: Where schemas live
docs.text:
Schemas are stored as Event Schemas inside an Event Schema Set in the Event Schema Registry. When you create a Business Event from Real-Time Hub, a schema is created automatically in the associated schema set.

To evolve a schema:

  1. Go to the Event Schema Set in the Event Schema Registry
  2. Open the schema you want to update
  3. Add, modify, or remove fields
  4. Save the new version — the platform increments the version number automatically

docs.title: What changes after a schema update
docs.text:
A schema update does not propagate automatically to publishers or consumers. Both sides must be updated explicitly.

flowchart TB
    A["<b>Update schema</b><br/>in Event Schema Registry"]
    B["<b>Update publisher</b><br/>to send new version"]
    C["<b>Create new consumer</b><br/>subscription for new version"]
    D["<b>Publisher</b> sends<br/>dataVersion v2"]
    E["<b>Consumer</b> receives<br/>v2 events"]

    A --> B
    A --> C
    B --> D
    C --> E

docs.title: Publisher update
docs.text:
The publisher must send the new dataVersion and include any new or changed fields in the payload:

# Before — v1
event_data = {
    "store_id": "STR-001",
    "product_id": "SKU-9821",
    "current_qty": 4
}
notebookutils.businessEvents.publish(
    workspace, schema_set, event_type, event_data, dataVersion="v1"
)

# After — v2 adds threshold_pct field
event_data = {
    "store_id": "STR-001",
    "product_id": "SKU-9821",
    "current_qty": 4,
    "threshold_pct": 0.15       # new field in v2
}
notebookutils.businessEvents.publish(
    workspace, schema_set, event_type, event_data, dataVersion="v2"
)

docs.title: Consumer update
docs.text:
Each consumer subscription is tied to a specific schema version. To consume the new version:

  • Activator — create a new alert rule targeting the updated Business Event
  • Eventhouse — a new KQL table is created for the new version; update your queries to reference it

Existing subscriptions keep receiving the old version

Subscriptions created for v1 continue to receive v1 events. They do not automatically upgrade to v2. You must create new subscriptions and migrate consumers deliberately.

docs.title: Versioning strategy
docs.text: Approach When to use Additive change (add new optional fields) Safe — existing consumers ignore unknown fields Breaking change (rename or remove fields) Requires new version and explicit consumer migration Parallel versions (run v1 and v2 simultaneously) Use during migration; decommission v1 once all consumers are updated

docs.title: Recommendations
docs.text:
Start with v1 from day one. Always publish with an explicit dataVersion so you have room to evolve without disruption.

Prefer additive changes. Adding new optional fields to a schema is the least disruptive path — consumers that do not need the new fields continue working without changes.

Communicate version changes to consumers. Because subscriptions do not auto-upgrade, consumer teams need to know when a new version is available so they can create updated subscriptions.

docs.title: Structuring Payloads
docs.text: A Business Event is more than a data record — it is a signal that something meaningful happened in your business. Designing a good payload means capturing enough context for any consumer to act on the event without needing to query additional systems.

docs.title: What makes a good business signal
docs.text:
A well-structured Business Event answers three questions:

Question Example field What happened? event_type: "Retail.Sales.VolumeAlert" What was involved? store_id, product_id, threshold_qty When and where? occurred_at, region

Keep payloads factual and immutable — describe what happened, not what should happen next. Decisions belong to the consumer, not the event.

docs.title: Anatomy of a Business Event schema
docs.text:
When you create a Business Event in Real-Time Hub, you define a schema with typed fields. These fields become the payload that publishers send and consumers receive.

{
  "store_id": "STR-001",
  "product_id": "SKU-9821",
  "current_qty": 4,
  "threshold_qty": 10,
  "occurred_at": "2024-11-15T14:32:00Z"
}

docs.title: Field type reference
docs.text: Type Use for string IDs, names, categories, status values int Counts, quantities, ranks float Prices, percentages, measurements boolean Flags, toggles

docs.title: CloudEvents under the hood
docs.text:
Business Events uses the CloudEvents specification as its envelope format. When you publish a payload, the platform wraps it automatically with standard metadata:

{
  "specversion": "1.0",
  "type": "Retail.Inventory.LowStockThreshold",
  "source": "/tenants/{tenant-id}/workspaces/{workspace-id}/items/{item-id}",
  "id": "a8f3c1d2-...",
  "time": "2024-11-15T14:32:00Z",
  "dataversion": "v1",
  "data": {
    "store_id": "STR-001",
    "product_id": "SKU-9821",
    "current_qty": 4,
    "threshold_qty": 10,
    "occurred_at": "2024-11-15T14:32:00Z"
  }
}

You only define and send the data block. The CloudEvents envelope (specversion, source, id, time) is added by the platform.

docs.title: What this means for consumers
docs.text:
• Activator receives the full CloudEvents envelope and lets you reference fields inside data directly in your alert conditions
  • Eventhouse stores the data fields as columns in the KQL table, with the envelope metadata available as additional columns

docs.title: Design guidelines
docs.text:
Include a timestamp in your payload. Even though the envelope has a time field, having occurred_at inside data lets you capture the business moment precisely — for example, when a transaction was processed, not when the event was published.

Use stable, opaque IDs. Field values like store_id or run_id should be identifiers that consumers can use to look up additional context if needed. Avoid embedding mutable state.

Keep payloads flat when possible. Nested objects are supported but make KQL queries and Activator field mapping more complex. Prefer flat structures unless nesting is semantically meaningful.

Version from the start. Always publish with dataVersion="v1". When the schema evolves, increment the version rather than changing existing fields. See Schema Versioning for details.

docs.title: Architecture Overview
docs.text:
Business Events separate the workload that recognizes a business condition from the workloads that respond. A warehouse shortage can become a purchasing request, for example, without the warehouse system taking responsibility for Fabric pipeline orchestration or the purchasing decision.

This page follows that low-stock handoff through its technical components, then shows how another finding can support independent operational and analytical responses.

docs.title: High-level architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    WMS["<b>Warehouse system</b><br/>Detects an item<br/>below its stock threshold"]
    UDF["<b>User Data Function</b><br/>Normalizes the<br/>shortage finding"]
    BE(["<b>Business Event</b><br/>Low-stock finding"])
    ACT["<b>Activator</b><br/>Starts request preparation<br/>for each finding"]
    P["<b>Data Pipeline</b><br/>Prepares a<br/>replenishment request"]
    R[("<b>Lakehouse Files</b><br/>Requests pending approval")]

    WMS -->|"Shortage facts"| UDF
    UDF -->|"Normalized finding"| BE
    BE -->|"Item and stock context"| ACT
    ACT -->|"Pipeline parameters"| P
    P -->|"Saved request"| R

The business contract is Retail.Inventory.LowStockThreshold. The warehouse retains its existing detection policy; the User Data Function adapts an already-detected finding to that contract rather than running a second stock test.

Responsibility Low-stock implementation Detect the condition The external warehouse system identifies the item and location below threshold. Share the finding A User Data Function sends the item, warehouse, stock, threshold, supplier context and observation time. Start the response Activator invokes the Data Pipeline with the original event fields. Produce reviewable work The pipeline saves a JSON request in Lakehouse Files with status pending_approval.

The outcome is a request ready for purchasing review, not an approved order or replenished inventory. The Low Stock Threshold Workbook provides the configuration and executable example.

Real-Time Hub is the entry point for creating and discovering the event and configuring its response. It is not another data-processing step, and the Event Schema Registry is not a runtime hop between the function and Activator.

docs.title: Event Schema Registry
docs.text:
The Event Schema Registry is the platform-level capability that holds schema definitions, organized into Event Schema Sets. For inventory, a schema set groups the contract used by the publishing function and its consumers. It does not contain stock records or purchasing requests.

flowchart TB
    subgraph Definition["Definition and organization, not runtime flow"]
        ESR["<b>Event Schema Registry</b><br/>Platform capability"]
        SS["<b>Inventory schema set</b><br/>Groups inventory contracts"]
        BE(["<b>Business Event schema</b><br/>Low-stock finding fields"])
        ESR ---|"Schema organization"| SS
        SS ---|"Contract definition"| BE
    end

Lines show schema organization, not event delivery. The schema for Retail.Inventory.LowStockThreshold defines the shortage payload; individual findings travel through the runtime path above.

Create the Business Event from Real-Time Hub → Business Events, selecting an existing Event Schema Set or creating one inline. Do not start from the Event Schema Registry. Configure the function's connection to that schema set and use the exact event type name when publishing.

docs.title: Publishers
docs.text:
A publisher supplies the shared finding. It can perform the detection itself or adapt a finding from an existing business system.

Publisher Example responsibility Notebook Compares expected and actual hourly store sales and shares each finding. User Data Function Normalizes a warehouse shortage without replacing warehouse detection. Eventstream Selects qualifying observations from a live stream and maps their fields to a business contract. Activator Shares a revenue exception recognized by an existing monitoring rule.

docs.title: Real-Time Hub
docs.text: The place to define and discover the Business Event and configure a response such as an Activator rule. Schema organization and consumer setup are configuration responsibilities, distinct from processing an individual shortage.

docs.title: Consumers
docs.text:
Workloads that subscribe to one or more Business Events and react when a matching event arrives.

Consumer Example responsibility Activator Starts replenishment-request preparation, or selects sales exceptions for a Teams notification. Eventstream Enriches a customer loyalty milestone with campaign reference data, filters eligible campaigns and writes candidates to Lakehouse Delta tables. Eventhouse Retains finding history for KQL analysis when Analyze in Eventhouse is enabled at creation.

Eventstream can be a publisher or a consumer, depending on the flow. In the Customer Loyalty Milestone scenario, it receives a Business Event as its source and prepares campaign candidates; it does not issue benefits. These Lakehouse Delta tables are response outputs, separate from optional managed Eventhouse history.

The pipeline and Lakehouse Files in the low-stock design implement the response started by Activator. The Lakehouse request is operational output, not the managed Eventhouse history of the Business Event.

docs.title: One event, multiple consumers
docs.text:
A store sales finding has two distinct uses: bringing a qualifying exception to operations and retaining the comparison for later analysis. Activator applies the notification threshold; Eventhouse history can retain findings independently of that threshold.

flowchart TB
    NB["<b>Sales Notebook</b><br/>Compares hourly<br/>store transactions"]
    BE(["<b>Business Event</b><br/>Store sales finding"])
    ACT["<b>Activator</b><br/>Selects deviations<br/>below -30%"]
    T["<b>Teams</b><br/>Operations receives<br/>the investigation context"]
    EH[("<b>Eventhouse</b><br/>Store finding history")]

    NB -->|"Store finding"| BE
    BE -->|"Deviation"| ACT
    ACT -->|"Sales exception"| T
    BE -.->|"Optional history"| EH

Both branches use Retail.Sales.VolumeAlert; neither waits for the other to complete. The dashed branch requires Analyze in Eventhouse at Business Event creation. It is not a mandatory stage before the Teams action, and recording an event is not evidence that operations investigated it.

Adding a response that uses the existing contract does not require changing the Notebook. Each consumer still needs its own configuration and outcome verification. If one response must wait for another to finish, use explicit orchestration rather than assuming fan-out provides that sequence.

docs.title: Design boundaries
docs.text:
• Detection stays with the source. A scheduled sales comparison remains scheduled; a warehouse finding does not require another stock detector in Fabric.
  • Facts and actions have different lifecycles. An accepted event, an Activator invocation and a saved request are different checkpoints. Verify the business output rather than treating publication as completion.
  • Responses must tolerate repeated delivery. Use the source finding identity to avoid unintended duplicate work; a schema does not provide exactly-once business processing.
  • Business decisions remain explicit. Preparing a replenishment request is not approving a purchase, just as a sales notification is not a completed investigation.

docs.title: Decision Guide
docs.text: Microsoft Fabric Real-Time Intelligence offers multiple ways to detect conditions, move data, and trigger responses. Start with what your existing implementation already does, then decide whether you also need a shared event contract. These capabilities can work together rather than replace one another.

docs.title: Capabilities at a glance
docs.text: Capability What it is Best for Business Events Schema-defined signals published by Fabric workloads to Real-Time Hub Discrete, meaningful occurrences that need to reach one or more consumers independently Eventstream High-throughput streaming pipeline for continuous data IoT telemetry, clickstreams, logs, and any high-volume continuous data Activator Rules engine that monitors data and triggers actions Reacting to conditions in streams or Business Events without writing code Direct API call HTTP call made from a Notebook or User Data Function to an external service When you need a synchronous response from a service outside Fabric

docs.title: Should I use Business Events?
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    A["<b>I need to signal</b> that<br/>something happened"]
    B{"Is it a continuous<br/>stream of data?"}
    Z1["<b>Use Eventstream</b>"]
    C{"Do other workloads<br/>need to act on this?"}
    E["<b>Use Business Events</b> ✅"]
    Z2["<b>Make a direct API call</b><br/>from a Notebook or UDF"]

    A --> B
    B -->|"Yes: high-volume, ongoing"| Z1
    B -->|"No: a discrete condition occurred"| C
    C -->|"Yes"| E
    C -->|"No: I need an immediate<br/>response to continue"| Z2

docs.title: When to use each option in Fabric
docs.text:
Use Business Events when:

  • A Notebook finishes a transformation and Activator or Eventhouse need to react
  • A threshold condition is detected and multiple consumers need to be notified independently
  • You want to add a new consumer without modifying the publisher
  • Multiple teams need a common representation of the same detected business condition
  • You need an explicit schema contract for the data the event carries

Use Eventstream when:

  • You are ingesting continuous data from IoT sensors, event producers, or external systems
  • You need to process or route high-volume data streams in real time
  • You need to process raw records before deciding which business conditions matter

Eventstream can also publish a Business Event when its processing detects a meaningful condition. The stream carries the underlying records; the Business Event represents the finding that other teams need.

Use Activator directly when:

  • You want to monitor an existing Eventstream or Eventhouse table for conditions
  • You need to trigger alerts or actions without publishing an explicit event
  • The logic lives entirely within Activator and no other consumer needs the signal

Make a direct API call when:

  • You are in a Notebook or User Data Function and need a synchronous response from an external service
  • The call is to a system outside Fabric (a REST API, a database, an external platform)
  • You need the result immediately to continue execution in the same workload

docs.title: Event Schema
docs.text: Every Business Event in Microsoft Fabric Real-Time Hub is defined by a schema before any data is published. The schema describes the structure and types of the event payload.

docs.title: What you define vs. what Real-Time Hub handles
docs.text:
Business Events are built on CloudEvents 1.0, an industry-standard specification for describing event data. However, you do not need to interact with the CloudEvents envelope directly. Real-Time Hub handles the transport layer for you.

Your responsibility is to define only the business properties of the event: what data it carries and what each field means.

Layer Managed by Example Transport envelope Real-Time Hub CloudEvents headers, routing, delivery Business payload You store_id, deviation_pct, severity

docs.title: Schema format
docs.text:
Business Events use a record schema with the following top-level structure:

{
  "type": "record",
  "name": "<EventName>",
  "fields": [
    {
      "name": "<field_name>",
      "type": "<field_type>",
      "doc": "<description>"
    }
  ]
}
Property Required Description type Yes Always "record" name Yes PascalCase name identifying the event type fields Yes Array of field definitions

docs.title: Field definition
docs.text:
Each field in the fields array has the following properties:

Property Required Description name Yes Field name (snake_case recommended) type Yes Data type of the field doc No Human-readable description of the field

docs.title: Supported field types
docs.text: Type Description Example value string UTF-8 text "store-mx-042" int 32-bit integer 1250 float 32-bit floating point -40.6 boolean True or false true

docs.title: Example schema
docs.text:
The following schema defines a Retail.Sales.VolumeAlert event with six fields. This JSON represents the schema you define when creating a Business Event in Real-Time Hub → Business Events. During creation, you can paste this directly into the code editor. If you need a new Event Schema Set, you can create one inline as part of the Business Event creation flow, or select an existing one.

{
  "type": "record",
  "name": "Retail.Sales.VolumeAlert",
  "fields": [
    {
      "name": "store_id",
      "type": "string",
      "doc": "Unique identifier of the store reporting the alert"
    },
    {
      "name": "expected_transactions",
      "type": "int",
      "doc": "Expected number of transactions based on historical average"
    },
    {
      "name": "actual_transactions",
      "type": "int",

docs.title: Schema naming conventions
docs.text: Convention Example name (event) PascalCase: VolumeAlert, LowStockThreshold name (field) snake_case: store_id, deviation_pct doc (field) Complete sentence describing the field's purpose and expected values

docs.title: Namespaces (optional but recommended)
docs.text:
For projects with multiple event types across different business domains, prefixing the event name with a namespace prevents naming collisions and makes the event's origin immediately clear.

The recommended pattern is Domain.Subdomain.EventName in PascalCase:

Without namespace With namespace VolumeAlert Retail.Sales.VolumeAlert LowStockThreshold Retail.Inventory.LowStockThreshold RunCompleted DataOps.Pipeline.RunCompleted

All examples in this repository follow the namespace convention.

docs.title: What are Business Events?
docs.text:
A Business Event is a named, schema-defined representation of a meaningful business occurrence or detected condition. It gives teams a shared contract for communicating situations such as inventory falling below a threshold, a shipment being delayed, or a customer reaching a loyalty milestone.

The business signal is the meaning of that situation. The Business Event is the shared record of a particular occurrence: which store, shipment or customer, what happened, and when. Existing notebooks, queries, rules and applications keep their detection logic; other workloads use the event to start a response or retain the finding for analysis.

Official documentation

For the complete API reference and platform overview, see the Business Events documentation on learn.microsoft.com.

docs.title: The core idea
docs.text:
Consider store operations monitoring hourly transaction volume. A sales Notebook already compares expected and actual transactions. Operations needs the stores with a significant drop brought to its attention, while analysts need the findings available for later comparison.

Instead of adding a Teams integration and a history-writing routine to the Notebook, the sales workload shares a Retail.Sales.VolumeAlert Business Event. Each occurrence carries the store, time window, expected transactions, actual transactions and deviation. Activator applies the operations response threshold; optional Eventhouse history retains the same findings independently.

The Notebook is the publisher: it supplies the business finding. Activator and Eventhouse are consumers: they use that finding for different purposes. These are responsibilities in the design, not additional steps that a business user must perform.

flowchart TB
    NB["<b>Sales Notebook</b><br/>Compares hourly<br/>store transactions"]
    BE(["<b>Business Event</b><br/>Store sales finding"])
    ACT["<b>Activator</b><br/>Selects deviations<br/>below -30%"]
    T["<b>Teams</b><br/>Operations receives<br/>the investigation context"]
    EH[("<b>Eventhouse</b><br/>Store finding history")]

    NB -->|"Store and sales figures"| BE
    BE -->|"Deviation"| ACT
    ACT -->|"Sales exception"| T
    BE -.->|"Optional history"| EH

Operations receives an investigation prompt only for deviations strictly below -30%; analysts can examine finding history when Analyze in Eventhouse is enabled at Business Event creation. Neither response changes the sales comparison or waits for the other. The event does not establish why sales fell or that anyone resolved the issue.

The Sales Volume Alert Workbook implements this example. Other publishers, including User Data Functions, Eventstream and Activator, serve different detection and integration needs; the Architecture Overview explains their roles.

docs.title: What makes the contract useful
docs.text:
Contract element Sales example Why it matters Named business meaning Retail.Sales.VolumeAlert Identifies a store sales finding, not merely a completed Notebook run. Subject and observation time store_id, window_start Keeps the response tied to the correct location and trading hour. Facts behind the finding expected_transactions, actual_transactions, deviation_pct Gives operations the original comparison rather than another request for an extract. Response policy Activator selects deviations below -30% Separates the sales measurement from the decision to notify operations.

Teams agree on the meaning, ownership and evolution of the contract. A schema enforces structure; it does not decide which findings deserve an action or make the business decision on a team's behalf.

docs.title: Key concepts
docs.text:
Schema-first design Define the Business Event in Real-Time Hub → Business Events before sending occurrences. Its typed record schema describes the shared facts. For the sales example, the meaning and unit of deviation_pct must remain consistent across the Notebook and Activator rule.

Decoupled architecture The Notebook does not call Teams or wait for historical analysis. A new response can reuse the existing contract without changing the sales calculation. Consumer configuration, permissions and verification are still required.

Real-time delivery Configured consumers react after a finding is published. An hourly Notebook still detects on its hourly schedule; event delivery does not make that calculation continuous or guarantee that the downstream action completed.

docs.title: Recipes
docs.text: Recipes are short, focused code snippets that solve one specific task. They are smaller than a full scenario — no business context, no architecture diagram — just the code you need.

docs.title: Available recipes
docs.text: Recipe Description Chain Two Business Events Use the output of one event as the trigger for another Batch Publish from a Notebook Publish multiple events in a single Notebook run Batch Publish from a User Data Function Publish multiple events from a UDF using an array payload

docs.title: Batch Publish from a Notebook
docs.text: Publish multiple Business Events in a single Notebook call — useful for processing a list of records and signaling each one as an individual business event.

docs.title: When to use this recipe
docs.text: Use batch publishing when your Notebook processes a collection of items and each item should generate its own event. For example, after a daily inventory check, publish one Retail.Inventory.LowStockThreshold event per product that is below threshold.

docs.title: Batch publish with an array payload
docs.text:
Pass a list of dictionaries as event_data to publish multiple events in a single call:

from datetime import datetime, timezone

low_stock_items = [
    {"product_id": "SKU-9821", "store_id": "STR-001", "current_qty": 4, "threshold_qty": 10},
    {"product_id": "SKU-4432", "store_id": "STR-003", "current_qty": 2, "threshold_qty": 15},
    {"product_id": "SKU-7751", "store_id": "STR-007", "current_qty": 1, "threshold_qty": 5},
]

event_data = [
    {**item, "occurred_at": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()}
    for item in low_stock_items
]

notebookutils.businessEvents.publish(
    "MyWorkspace",
    "RetailInventory",
    "Retail.Inventory.LowStockThreshold",
    event_data,
    dataVersion="v1"
)

docs.title: Considerations
docs.text:
Publish only what changed. Filter your dataset before building the array — include only items that crossed a threshold, not every item in the inventory.

Each item in the array becomes an independent event. The platform delivers each one individually, with its own retry window.

Avoid very large arrays. If you need to publish thousands of events per second, consider using Eventstream with a streaming source instead of a Notebook call.

docs.title: Batch Publish from a User Data Function
docs.text: Publish multiple Business Events in a single User Data Function call by passing an array as the event data.

docs.title: When to use this recipe
docs.text: Use batch publishing from a UDF when your function processes a collection of items and each item should generate its own event — for example, when multiple inventory updates arrive together and each one should produce an independent event.

docs.title: Batch publish with an array payload
docs.text:
The key difference from a single-event publish is that event_data is a list of dictionaries instead of a single dictionary:

import fabric.functions as fn
import json
from datetime import datetime, timezone

udf = fn.UserDataFunctions()

@udf.connection(argName="businessEventsClient", alias="RetailInventory")
@udf.function()
def batch_publish(
    businessEventsClient: fn.FabricBusinessEventsClient,
    items_json: str
) -> str:
    items = json.loads(items_json)

    event_data = [
        {
            "store_id": item["store_id"],
            "product_id": item["product_id"],
            "current_qty": item["current_qty"],
            "threshold_qty": item["threshold_qty"],
            "occurred_at": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()
        }
        for item in items
    ]

    businessEventsClient.PublishEvent(
        type="Retail.Inventory.LowStockThreshold",
        event_data=event_data,
        data_version="v1"
    )

    return f"Published {len(event_data)} events"

docs.title: Example input
docs.text:
Pass a JSON string as the items_json parameter when calling the function:

[
  { "store_id": "STR-001", "product_id": "SKU-9821", "current_qty": 4, "threshold_qty": 10 },
  { "store_id": "STR-003", "product_id": "SKU-4432", "current_qty": 2, "threshold_qty": 15 },
  { "store_id": "STR-007", "product_id": "SKU-7751", "current_qty": 1, "threshold_qty": 5 }
]

docs.title: Add error handling
docs.text:
import fabric.functions as fn
import json
from datetime import datetime, timezone

udf = fn.UserDataFunctions()

@udf.connection(argName="businessEventsClient", alias="RetailInventory")
@udf.function()
def batch_publish(
    businessEventsClient: fn.FabricBusinessEventsClient,
    items_json: str
) -> str:
    try:
        items = json.loads(items_json)
    except (ValueError, TypeError):
        return "Invalid JSON input"

    if not isinstance(items, list) or len(items) == 0:
        return "Input must be a non-empty array"

    event_data = [
        {
            "store_id": item["store_id"],
            "product_id": item["product_id"],
            "current_qty": item["current_qty"],
            "threshold_qty": item["threshold_qty"],
            "occurred_at": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()
        }
        for item in items
    ]

    businessEventsClient.PublishEvent(
        type="Retail.Inventory.LowStockThreshold",
        event_data=event_data,
        data_version="v1"
    )

    return f"Published {len(event_data)} events"

docs.title: Considerations
docs.text:
Each item in the array becomes an independent event. The platform delivers each one individually, with its own retry window.

Validate array size before publishing. Very large arrays may hit request size limits. Filter the input to only include items that actually need an event.

docs.title: Chain Two Business Events
docs.text: Use the output of one Business Event as the trigger for publishing a second Business Event. This creates a lightweight event chain where each step signals the next.

docs.title: When to use this recipe
docs.text: Use event chaining when a business process has sequential stages and each stage has independent consumers. Chaining keeps each stage loosely coupled — the first publisher does not need to know what happens next.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    P1["<b>Publisher</b><br/>Notebook"]
    E1["<b>Business Event A</b><br/>Order.Processing.Completed"]
    ACT["<b>Activator</b><br/>Monitors Event A"]
    P2["<b>Activator</b> publishes"]
    E2["<b>Business Event B</b><br/>Order.Fulfillment.Started"]
    C1["<b>Eventhouse</b><br/>Fulfillment analytics"]
    C2["<b>Activator</b><br/>Notify warehouse"]

    P1 -->|"Publishes"| E1
    E1 --> ACT
    ACT -->|"Condition met"| P2
    P2 -->|"Publishes"| E2
    E2 --> C1
    E2 --> C2

docs.title: Step 1: Publish the first event
docs.text:
# Notebook publishes Event A when order processing completes
event_data = {
    "order_id": "ORD-4421",
    "customer_id": "CUST-882",
    "total_amount": 340.00,
    "completed_at": "2024-11-15T14:32:00Z"
}

notebookutils.businessEvents.publish(
    "MyWorkspace",
    "OrderProcessing",
    "Order.Processing.Completed",
    event_data,
    dataVersion="v1"
)

docs.title: Step 2: Configure Activator to publish Event B
docs.text:
1. Go to Real-Time Hub → Business events
  2. Find Order.Processing.Completed and click Set alert
  3. Configure Monitor: source = Order.Processing.Completed
  4. Configure Condition: On each value
  5. Configure Action: Publish a business event
  6. Select Order.Fulfillment.Started as the target event
  7. Map fields from Event A to Event B:
Event A field Event B field order_id order_id customer_id customer_id (static value) started_at → current timestamp

docs.title: Design considerations
docs.text:
Keep chains short. Each hop adds latency and a potential failure point. If you need more than 2-3 steps, consider whether an orchestration tool (Data Pipeline, Power Automate) is a better fit.

Each event should be independently meaningful. If Event B is only ever triggered by Event A and has no other consumers, evaluate whether two separate events are necessary.

Do not create circular chains. Event A triggering Event B triggering Event A will cause an infinite loop. Design chains to always move forward in the process.

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text: Choose the business outcome you want to explore: bring a finding to someone's attention, prepare work for a team, or understand recurring activity. Open the scenario for its business context and architecture, then use its Workbook for preparation, connections and one complete exercise. Some responses require connections to your own business systems.

docs.title: How to read a scenario
docs.text:
Each scenario has two pages with one shared outcome:

  1. Business context: how the activity works today, the current problem, what changes with Business Events, and the event-driven architecture with its flows explained. The page also states what the exercise demonstrates and where it stops.
  2. Workbook: prerequisites, resource coverage, supported deployment or manual preparation, required connections, one source sample and visible results, including cases that should be ignored.

Schemas, mappings, KQL, SQL and source examples are retained in the Workbook, next to the relevant step or in expandable implementation reference. Optional extensions are separate from completion criteria.

Level reflects the Workbook's manual setup and result-checking effort:

  • Beginner: few setup steps and straightforward result checks.
  • Intermediate: some manual setup or guided result checks.
  • Advanced: substantial manual setup or coordinated, multi-step checks.

Scenarios are ordered by level within each pattern, with advanced exercises last.

docs.title: Track & Analyze
docs.text:
Use this pattern when the primary outcome is understanding received business activity rather than starting an operational response. Order History Analysis compares synthetic orders across two stores.

Scenario Industry Publisher Consumer(s) Level Workbook Order History Analysis Retail Notebook Eventhouse Beginner Workbook

With Analyze in Eventhouse enabled during Business Event creation, received events are automatically persisted in a dedicated KQL table. This history consumer is required for Order History Analysis, whose Workbook guides native setup and one result query; it does not claim automated provisioning. History remains an optional extension in the operational scenarios, and their deployment packages do not configure it. A source Eventhouse is not the same as an event-history destination.

Good first scenario

Start with Order History Analysis for a Beginner publish-and-query exercise. Choose Sales Volume Alert when you are ready to connect an operational response in Teams.

Combine patterns

Add received-event analysis when it answers a business question, such as recurring sales drops or repeated stock shortages. Plan the history choice when creating the event, and check delivered messages, saved requests or cases separately. A history row does not establish that an operational action completed.

docs.title: Detect & Alert
docs.text:
Use this pattern when a finding needs a person's attention. Sales Volume Alert notifies store operations in Teams. Revenue Below Target prepares the figures a revenue team needs for commercial review. Eventhouse can separately retain the findings to help teams identify recurring patterns.

Scenario Industry Publisher Consumer(s) Level Workbook Sales Volume Alert Retail Notebook Activator (Teams), optional Eventhouse Intermediate Workbook Revenue Below Target Sales Activator (Business Event publication) Activator (Data Pipeline), optional Eventhouse Advanced Workbook

docs.title: Decide & Act
docs.text:
Use this pattern to turn a finding or decision into work. Prepare a replenishment request, register a payment review case, or apply an order hold. Each team owns its response to the shared signal. The scenario makes clear where the work stops: a request still needs approval, and a review case still needs assessment. Add another response without changing the publisher.

Scenario Industry Publisher Consumer(s) Level Workbook Low Stock Threshold Supply Chain User Data Function Activator (Data Pipeline), optional Eventhouse Intermediate Workbook Real-Time Stream Alert Finance Eventstream Activator (User Data Function), optional Eventhouse Intermediate Workbook Discount Approval Evaluation and Event Publication Sales User Data Function Activator (Teams), Eventstream, optional Eventhouse Intermediate Workbook Real-Time Viewer Recommendations Media User Data Function Activator (User Data Function), optional Eventhouse Intermediate Workbook Data Pipeline Failure Follow-up DataOps Notebook Activator (User Data Function), optional Eventhouse Intermediate Workbook Customer Loyalty Milestone Retail Activator Eventstream (campaign enrichment → Lakehouse Delta tables) Advanced Workbook Abandoned Cart Recovery Ecommerce User Data Function Activator (Power Automate: email and SQL follow-up), optional Eventhouse Advanced Workbook Fraud Response Before Fulfillment Finance User Data Function Activator (Power Automate), optional Eventhouse Advanced Workbook

The fan-out advantage

Fraud Response Before Fulfillment uses one event to support three separate responses. Teams can evolve their workflows without changing the publisher, while still agreeing how competing or overlapping actions should be handled.

docs.title: Business Context
docs.text:
The storefront already identifies abandoned carts and retains the cart identity, customer details, value and time of abandonment. The recovery team uses those records to prepare customer reminders and to organize commercial follow-up. Those activities share the same starting facts, but they serve different purposes and do not have the same eligibility rules.

Here, reminder preparation selects the carts that merit an email, while the team separately maintains a register of cart-level tasks. Staff must reconcile those two views rather than assume that everyone receiving an email represents all the work to be done. A lower-value cart still needs a task, and two carts belonging to one customer are two separate opportunities to follow up. The risk is incomplete coverage, not simply a missing email.

    M["<b>Email channel</b><br/>Delivers customer reminders"]
    subgraph GAP["Gap: Some carts can miss<br/>their own follow-up task"]
        F["<b>Recovery team</b><br/>Reconciles tasks<br/>for every cart"]:::businessGap
    end
    T[("<b>Task register</b><br/>Individual carts")]
    S -->|"Cart details"| C
    C -->|"Select candidates"| E
    E -->|"Send reminder"| M
    C -->|"Cart context"| F
    F -->|"Record tasks"| T
    classDef businessGap fill:#FFF4CE,stroke:#C88700,color:#000000
    style GAP fill:none,stroke:#C88700,stroke-width:1.5px

docs.title: Current Problem
docs.text:
Reminder eligibility and follow-up coverage are not the same policy. If the reminder list is treated as the complete worklist, lower-value carts disappear from follow-up. If work is recorded only against the customer, separate carts can lose their individual context.

The team needs selective outreach and a complete cart-level task register, both based on the abandonment the storefront already identified.

docs.title: Improved Business Response
docs.text:
One response sends reminders for qualifying cart values; another registers a follow-up task for every valid cart, keeping different carts from the same customer separate. The storefront's abandonment finding is published as a Business Event and reaches these two independent responses.

flowchart TB
    S["<b>Storefront</b><br/>Identifies abandoned carts"]
    E(["<b>Business Event</b><br/>Individual cart abandonment"])
    M["<b>Customer outreach</b><br/>Sends reminders for<br/>cart values above 30"]
    subgraph VALUE["Improvement: Every valid cart gets<br/>its own follow-up task"]
        F["<b>Commercial follow-up</b><br/>Registers each cart<br/>as a separate task"]:::businessValue
        T[("<b>Task register</b><br/>Cart-specific context")]:::businessValue
    end
    S -->|"Share cart context"| E
    E -->|"Apply reminder policy"| M
    E -->|"Every valid cart"| F
    F -->|"Preserve each cart separately"| T
    classDef businessValue fill:#DFF6DD,stroke:#107C10,color:#000000
    style VALUE fill:none,stroke:#107C10,stroke-width:1.5px

The recovery team can apply different policies to customer communication and internal work without recreating abandonment detection. A reminder does not have to finish before a task is registered, and the task register does not determine who receives an email. The result is organized recovery work, not evidence of recovered revenue.

docs.text:
Business signal: Ecommerce.Cart.Abandoned

Publisher: User Data Function | Consumer(s): Activator (Power Automate: email and SQL follow-up)

The reminder and task branches proceed independently after publication:

  1. The publishing User Data Function validates the storefront's cart facts and shares the abandonment as a Business Event.
  2. One Activator rule selects cart values strictly above 30 and invokes the Power Automate reminder flow, which delivers to the approved mailbox.
  3. A separate Activator rule responds to every valid cart and invokes the SQL follow-up flow, preserving a task for that individual cart.

Use an approved test mailbox and the writable SQL database. The task register represents follow-up work, not a complete CRM application.

Dashed arrows show optional event history and its analysis, separate from the required response. Analyze in Eventhouse is a creation-time choice, not a connection enabled by the deployment package or a prerequisite for completing the Workbook.

docs.title: Business outcome and boundaries
docs.text:
From six synthetic carts, deliver three reminders for values strictly above 30 and create six SQL follow-up tasks. Different carts from the same customer remain separate tasks.

Where the exercise stops: Exact 30, below-threshold and zero-value carts create tasks but no reminder. This exercise does not calculate offers, recover orders or prove revenue recovery. Real outreach also needs current cart state, contact preferences and approved eligibility checks.

docs.text: The Workbook brings preparation, connections, sample inputs, expected results and code reference into one place. Follow that single path to explore the outcome above.

docs.title: Business Context
docs.text:
The loyalty program maintains customer-wide spending and tier information across stores. Marketing works from a separate campaign catalog that identifies which campaigns are available for each tier and store, whether they are active and which benefits they offer. A customer's progress through the program and the availability of a local campaign are different business facts.

For the current process in this scenario, loyalty operations identifies a new Gold milestone and marketing prepares the campaign candidates. A planner must match the customer's tier and store to the catalog, exclude inactive campaigns and keep missing matches available for review. This is more than exporting customers above a spending threshold: a spending list alone does not tell marketing which campaign it can prepare, and an unresolved catalog entry must not look like a customer ready for outreach.

A customer passing the Gold spending threshold does not identify a usable campaign. The relevant campaign may be active, inactive or missing from the catalog. A list based on spending alone leaves marketing checking those distinctions or preparing outreach for an unavailable campaign.

Missing campaign mappings also need a visible review path rather than disappearing into the same list. Continued spending above the threshold should not be mistaken for a new milestone.

docs.text:
Business signal: Retail.Customer.MilestoneReached

Publisher: Activator | Consumer(s): Eventstream (campaign enrichment and Lakehouse Delta tables)

    PUB["<b>Activator</b><br/>Detects spending crossings<br/>above 5000 USD"]
    BE(["<b>Business Event</b><br/>Retail.Customer.MilestoneReached"])
    ES["<b>Eventstream</b><br/>Joins tier and store<br/>to the campaign catalog"]
    REF[("<b>Lakehouse reference table</b><br/>Campaigns and<br/>benefit codes")]

  4. The two Lakehouse Delta tables make campaign preparation and missing-mapping review available separately to marketing.

The source Eventhouse holds supplied balances; this exercise does not calculate lifetime spend. No consumer Activator, CRM change, issued reward or delivered communication is part of the outcome.

docs.title: Business Context
docs.text:
Data operations runs workloads and inspects execution records to understand which loads completed, which were skipped and which failed. The records contain the workload identity, outcome, processed-row count and failure context. A successful load can legitimately contain no rows, while a failed load may already have processed part of its input.

In the current workflow here, an operator reviews those records, identifies a failed workload and prepares a case for the team responsible for investigation. The case needs the individual workload's context, not just the overall job status or a generic failure message. Until the error and progress are carried into the triage register, the next person must reconstruct what happened. Completed and deliberately skipped work should remain visible without creating competing incident work.

flowchart TB
    W["<b>Data workload</b><br/>Runs the data load"]
    L[("<b>Execution records</b><br/>Workload and outcome<br/>Processed rows")]
    subgraph GAP["Gap: Failure records are not<br/>ready-to-triage cases"]
        O{"Did operations find<br/>a failed workload?"}:::businessGap
        P["<b>Triage preparation</b><br/>Captures error and<br/>processed-row count"]:::businessGap
    end
    C[("<b>Triage register</b><br/>Workload-level cases")]
    N["<b>Execution history</b><br/>Completed or<br/>skipped workloads"]
    W -->|"Record outcome"| L
    L -->|"Inspect"| O
    O -->|"Failed"| P
    P -->|"Register case"| C
    O -->|"Completed or skipped"| N
    classDef businessGap fill:#FFF4CE,stroke:#C88700,color:#000000
    style GAP fill:none,stroke:#C88700,stroke-width:1.5px

docs.title: Current Problem
docs.text:
Execution history is a record of what happened, not a ready-made triage queue. If failures stay only in that history, someone must collect the workload identity and progress before handing the problem to the next person.

Treating every outcome as an incident creates the opposite problem: successful empty loads and intentional skips compete with failures for attention. The business needs actionable follow-up without losing the detail of partial progress.

docs.title: Improved Business Response
docs.text:
The follow-up response selects failed workload outcomes and creates a case containing the workload identity, failure context and processed-row count. Each workload outcome is shared as a Business Event. Completed and skipped work does not enter the triage queue.

flowchart TB
    W["<b>Workload execution</b><br/>Records each<br/>workload outcome"]
    E(["<b>Business Event</b><br/>Individual workload outcome"])
    subgraph VALUE["Improvement: Failures arrive as cases<br/>with their error and progress"]
        F["<b>Failure follow-up</b><br/>Selects failed workloads"]:::businessValue
        C[("<b>Triage register</b><br/>Workload, error and<br/>processed-row count")]:::businessValue
    end
    O["<b>Operations team</b><br/>Reviews cases<br/>for investigation"]
    W -->|"Share outcome"| E
    E -->|"Apply follow-up policy"| F
    F -->|"Register failure context"| C
    C -->|"Make case available"| O
    classDef businessValue fill:#DFF6DD,stroke:#107C10,color:#000000
    style VALUE fill:none,stroke:#107C10,stroke-width:1.5px

Operations can begin with a case ready for investigation rather than reconstructing the execution history. The team responsible for follow-up can change how cases are prepared without changing the data workload. Registering the failure is the handoff to triage, not a repair or rerun of the failed work.

docs.title: Discount Approval Evaluation and Event Publication
Business Context
docs.text:
A seller prepares a commercial proposal using its pricing, discount and cost context. The pricing policy evaluates the requested discount and resulting margin, distinguishing deals within policy from those requiring manager or executive review. The seller receives that evaluation while still working on the proposal.

The operating model here leaves the next step with the seller: when review is needed, the proposal facts and policy reason must be prepared for the review team. The manager or executive needs to understand both the commercial request and why it falls outside the normal policy. A result on the seller's screen is not yet a review request in the team's worklist, and asking the receiving team to calculate the requirement again can produce competing interpretations of the same deal.

flowchart TB
    P[("<b>Proposal records</b><br/>Pricing and costs")]
    E["<b>Pricing policy</b><br/>Evaluates discount<br/>and margin"]
    subgraph GAP["Gap: The policy result still needs<br/>to reach the review team"]
        S["<b>Seller</b><br/>Reads the review requirement"]:::businessGap
        C["<b>Review request preparation</b><br/>Captures proposal<br/>and policy reason"]:::businessGap
    end
    Q[("<b>Review worklist</b><br/>Required review level")]
    R["<b>Manager or executive</b><br/>Reviews the policy exception"]
    P -->|"Evaluate"| E
    E -->|"Policy result"| S
    S -->|"Review required"| C
    C -->|"Register request"| Q
    Q -->|"Review proposal"| R
    classDef businessGap fill:#FFF4CE,stroke:#C88700,color:#000000
    style GAP fill:none,stroke:#C88700,stroke-width:1.5px

docs.title: Current Problem
docs.text:
A result visible only to the seller does not bring the proposal to the review team's attention. Copying the details into another channel leaves the team reconstructing why review was requested.

If each follow-up process also interprets the policy separately, the same proposal can acquire different review requirements. The business needs one evaluation to inform both the seller and the people who will consider the exception.

docs.title: Improved Business Response
docs.text:
The proposal is evaluated once and the result is returned to the seller. When manager or executive review is required, the same result is shared as a Business Event with the proposal context and reason. Within-policy proposals do not create review notifications.

flowchart TB
    P["<b>Pricing policy</b><br/>Evaluates discount<br/>and margin"]
    S["<b>Seller</b><br/>Receives the policy result"]
    D{"Is manager or executive<br/>review required?"}
    E(["<b>Business Event</b><br/>Review requirement"])
    subgraph VALUE["Improvement: The review team receives<br/>the proposal and policy reason"]
        R["<b>Review team</b><br/>Receives proposal facts<br/>and the policy reason"]:::businessValue
    end
    F["<b>Independent follow-up</b><br/>Receives the same<br/>review requirement"]
    P -->|"Return evaluation"| S
    P -->|"Check follow-up need"| D
    D -->|"Review required"| E
    E -->|"Notify review team"| R
    E -->|"Share independently"| F
    classDef businessValue fill:#DFF6DD,stroke:#107C10,color:#000000
    style VALUE fill:none,stroke:#107C10,stroke-width:1.5px

The seller gets an answer without waiting for every follow-up response, and the review team gets the reasoning it needs rather than another policy to interpret. Other uses of the review requirement can be added independently. The shared result identifies a need for review, not an approval already granted.

docs.title: Business Context
docs.text:
An online retailer receives orders and scores from an existing risk-scoring process. Its policy uses the supplied score and order context to determine whether an order can be released, needs human review or should be held. The warehouse, however, follows the fulfillment permission saved in the order system rather than the separate risk assessment.

In the current process described here, order operations must take the recorded policy decision and apply it to the order before the warehouse can rely on it. Risk review and fulfillment can therefore be looking at different records of the same order. A warning that has reached a person is not equivalent to a hold that the warehouse enforces, and requesting a review does not mean that a reviewer has cleared the order for release.

flowchart TB
    S["<b>Risk input</b><br/>Order and supplied score"]
    P["<b>Risk policy</b><br/>Selects hold, review<br/>or release"]
    R[("<b>Risk assessment</b><br/>Score and decision")]
    subgraph GAP["Gap: Risk decisions are not yet<br/>enforced by the order system"]
        O["<b>Order operations</b><br/>Applies the risk decision"]:::businessGap
        OMS[("<b>Order system</b><br/>Order state and<br/>fulfillment permission")]:::businessGap
    end
    W["<b>Warehouse</b><br/>Checks fulfillment<br/>permission"]
    S -->|"Evaluate"| P
    P -->|"Record"| R
    R -->|"Operations action"| O
    O -->|"Save state"| OMS
    OMS -->|"Check permission"| W
    classDef businessGap fill:#FFF4CE,stroke:#C88700,color:#000000
    style GAP fill:none,stroke:#C88700,stroke-width:1.5px

docs.title: Current Problem
docs.text:
A risk decision recorded separately from order operations may leave fulfillment permission unchanged. Sending a warning does not prevent an order from proceeding, and a request for human review must not be mistaken for a completed review.

The missing connection is from the policy decision to an actual order-state change, with distinct handling for hold, review and release.

docs.title: Improved Business Response
docs.text:
The connected response applies a hold, requests review or releases the order. The order system saves that result and enforces the corresponding fulfillment permission. The risk-policy result is published as a Business Event for the order so the relevant response can apply it.

flowchart TB
    P["<b>Risk policy</b><br/>Uses the supplied score<br/>and order context"]
    E(["<b>Business Event</b><br/>Order risk decision"])
    subgraph VALUE["Improvement: Risk decisions reach<br/>the system that controls fulfillment"]
        H["<b>Hold response</b><br/>Requests an order hold"]:::businessValue
        V["<b>Review response</b><br/>Requests human review"]:::businessValue
        L["<b>Release response</b><br/>Requests order release"]:::businessValue
        O["<b>Order system</b><br/>Saves the state and enforces<br/>fulfillment permission"]:::businessValue
    end
    P -->|"Share policy result"| E
    E -->|"Hold"| H
    E -->|"Review"| V
    E -->|"Release"| L
    H -->|"Block fulfillment"| O
    V -->|"Keep blocked pending review"| O
    L -->|"Permit fulfillment"| O
    classDef businessValue fill:#DFF6DD,stroke:#107C10,color:#000000
    style VALUE fill:none,stroke:#107C10,stroke-width:1.5px

This makes the policy useful at the point where operational behavior changes: released orders can proceed, while held and review-requested orders remain blocked. Business Events carries the decision to that response; it does not replace the connected order system or perform the human review.

The Workbook checks the saved order states and fulfillment behavior separately from event delivery.

Where the exercise stops: A supplied score is not proof of fraud. review_requested is not review_completed. You must supply an authenticated, isolated test order system and connect the three real responses; the package does not deploy an order backend.

docs.title: Business Context
docs.text:
The warehouse management system tracks available stock and identifies items below their replenishment threshold. Its shortage record already contains the item, warehouse, observed stock, threshold and supplier context. Warehouse operations owns that finding; the replenishment team owns deciding what purchasing response should follow.

Here, a replenishment coordinator takes the shortage details from the warehouse system and prepares a request for the purchasing team. The reviewer needs the original stock position and observation time to understand why the request exists. Until that request is recorded, a shortage can be visible to the warehouse without being present in the approval queue. Copying the facts does not replenish stock, but it determines whether the purchasing decision is ready to be made.

flowchart TB
    S[("<b>Inventory records</b><br/>Item, stock and threshold")]
    W["<b>Warehouse system</b><br/>Detects low stock"]
    subgraph GAP["Gap: Shortages are not yet<br/>in the approval queue"]
        C["<b>Replenishment team</b><br/>Transfers shortage facts"]:::businessGap
        P["<b>Request preparation</b><br/>Captures item, warehouse,<br/>supplier and time"]:::businessGap
    end
    Q[("<b>Request register</b><br/>Pending approval")]
    R["<b>Purchasing team</b><br/>Reviews replenishment<br/>requests"]
    S -->|"Monitor stock"| W
    W -->|"Shortage details"| C
    C -->|"Copy facts"| P
    P -->|"Save request"| Q
    Q -->|"Review work"| R
    classDef businessGap fill:#FFF4CE,stroke:#C88700,color:#000000
    style GAP fill:none,stroke:#C88700,stroke-width:1.5px

docs.title: Current Problem
docs.text:
A shortage can be visible in the warehouse system without a corresponding request being ready for replenishment to review. When the details must be transferred separately, the team first reconstructs the finding instead of assessing the response.

Repeating the stock check in the request process also creates two places to interpret the shortage policy. The missing step is preparing reviewable work from a finding that the warehouse has already made.

docs.title: Improved Business Response
docs.text:
Each low-stock finding starts preparation of a saved replenishment request using the original item, location and stock context. The request is available for approval rather than remaining a shortage observation in another system. The warehouse finding is shared as a low-stock Business Event.

flowchart TB
    W["<b>Warehouse system</b><br/>Detects low stock"]
    E(["<b>Business Event</b><br/>Low-stock finding"])
    subgraph VALUE["Improvement: Shortages become<br/>requests ready for approval review"]
        P["<b>Request preparation</b><br/>Uses the original<br/>shortage facts"]:::businessValue
        Q[("<b>Replenishment requests</b><br/>Pending approval")]:::businessValue
    end
    R["<b>Purchasing team</b><br/>Reviews the<br/>prepared request"]
    W -->|"Share shortage"| E
    E -->|"Start request preparation"| P
    P -->|"Save original context"| Q
    Q -->|"Make reviewable work available"| R
    classDef businessValue fill:#DFF6DD,stroke:#107C10,color:#000000
    style VALUE fill:none,stroke:#107C10,stroke-width:1.5px

Replenishment can focus on the next purchasing decision instead of re-entering the details. The warehouse keeps its established detection policy, while the team can change how it prepares requests without introducing another stock test.

docs.text:
A retail operations analyst compares accepted orders across stores to understand order volume and value. The order system records each order, while the analyst works from periodic exports. This example starts with two stores and a small set of synthetic orders; it does not assume an integration with a real retailer.

Repeating the export also makes it easy to mix different runs of a learning exercise or count the same order more than once.

docs.text:
An independent history consumer records accepted order findings so the analyst can compare stores without requesting a new export from the publisher. Each accepted order is shared as a Business Event with a consistent meaning. A run identifier separates exercises, and an order identifier supports counting each order once within a run.

docs.title: Business Context
docs.text:
Retail payments arrive continuously, and the payments system retains the transaction identity, amount, currency, store and processing time. Payment operations applies a review policy to identify transactions that deserve closer assessment. The reviewer works from a case, not from the full transaction feed.

The current process in this scenario requires the selected payment to be copied into a review register before that assessment can begin. The person preparing the case must keep the original amount and currency together; a large number in one currency is not a comparable risk score across all currencies. Identifying a qualifying payment and making it available to a reviewer are therefore two distinct responsibilities, and the second can remain unfinished even when the first has succeeded.

flowchart TB
    P["<b>Payments system</b><br/>Records incoming payments"]
    L[("<b>Transaction records</b><br/>Amount and currency<br/>Store and time")]
    subgraph GAP["Gap: Selected payments still need<br/>a recorded review case"]
        O["<b>Payment operations</b><br/>Selects payments<br/>for review"]:::businessGap
        C["<b>Case preparation</b><br/>Captures original<br/>transaction facts"]:::businessGap
    end
    Q[("<b>Review cases</b><br/>Pending assessment")]
    R["<b>Payment reviewer</b><br/>Assesses the transaction"]
    P -->|"Record"| L
    L -->|"Review activity"| O
    O -->|"Selected payments"| C
    C -->|"Register case"| Q
    Q -->|"Assess case"| R
    classDef businessGap fill:#FFF4CE,stroke:#C88700,color:#000000
    style GAP fill:none,stroke:#C88700,stroke-width:1.5px

docs.title: Current Problem
docs.text:
The payment activity can contain a qualifying transaction without a case appearing in the review queue. Asking reviewers to search the wider activity and copy payment details leaves a gap between identifying a review condition and organizing the work.

A separate process that interprets the amount condition again can also select a different population. Review needs a consistent finding with its original currency, not an assumption that a large payment is fraudulent.

docs.text:

A viewing application records watches, likes, clicks, searches and skips with the viewer, content and session context. A separate recommendation process uses a content catalog to prepare suggestions. The product team must decide which interactions express enough interest to justify refreshing those suggestions, rather than treating every action as equally meaningful.

In this operating model, application-specific logic connects recorded interactions to requests for a new list. It must choose the relevant action and carry the right viewer and session context into recommendation preparation. Collecting more interaction history does not, on its own, make a refreshed list available. Finance and regional leaders monitor revenue against the target for each region and reporting period. A performance view shows the latest revenue, target and variance, while the underlying observations retain how that position has changed. The same region can stay below plan through several updates, recover and then fall behind again.

In this scenario, a finance analyst decides whether the latest observation warrants a new investigation, then assembles the figures for regional review. That decision requires more than the current percentage: the analyst must distinguish a continuing issue from a renewed decline and retain the values that prompted concern. Otherwise, each refresh can create more work for the same shortfall, or a later decline can be dismissed as something the team is already investigating.

Finance also needs the figures that prompted the concern, not just whatever values happen to be displayed when someone begins the review.
