docs.title: Abandoned Cart Recovery: Workbook
docs.text:
Business context and architecture | Download package | Implementation

Help the recovery team act on abandoned carts: send a reminder for carts above 30 and create a follow-up task for every cart. Set up the sample, connect your approved mailbox and SQL database, then check both outcomes.

docs.title: Resources and coverage
docs.text:
Component Default name Package coverage Event schema and delegated Publish/Consume permissions CartSchema Public preview; original six-field Ecommerce.Cart.Abandoned contract Native User Data Function publisher CartPublisher Managed schema connection and six camelCase inputs; publishes the original snake_case fields Activator event source CartActions Native Business Event connection and prepared Cart abandonment events event SQL database in Fabric CartFollowUp Holds follow-up tasks; execute the two included SQL scripts before testing Recovery email rule and Power Automate flow Cart Recovery - Email Manual custom action, mappings, flow connection and activation; strict cart_value > 30 SQL follow-up rule and Power Automate flow Cart Recovery - SQL Follow-up Manual custom action, mappings and stored-procedure action; every valid cart Approved mailbox and SQL connector identity Learner-owned Manual connection permissions; the SQL script supplies two synthetic customers, never real customer data Independent managed event history Not configured by this package Creation-time option; see Optional event history Storefront, profile store and offer engine Not configured by this package No inactivity detection, profile lookup, discount calculation or conversion measurement

The package creates four Fabric items. Complete the SQL setup and connect the two Power Automate flows in Step 3 before sending carts. The database is a follow-up register for the team, not a complete CRM application.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text: Use Python 3.10+, Azure CLI and PowerShell on Windows, an active supported Fabric capacity, and permission to create the scenario's workspace items and execute its source. Prepare any learner-owned connections listed in the coverage table.

docs.title: 1. Configure your environment
docs.text:
Download abandoned-cart-recovery.zip or the repository ZIP, extract it, and open its cicd\abandoned-cart-recovery folder.

Replace the three placeholders below:

Set-Location '<extracted-folder>\cicd\abandoned-cart-recovery'
$tenantId = '<your-tenant-uuid>'
$workspaceId = '<your-workspace-uuid>'

az login --tenant $tenantId
python .\deploy.py configure --tenant-id $tenantId --workspace-id $workspaceId --auth-provider azure_cli --output .\config.local.json

Review the tenant, workspace and unused resource names in config.local.json. accept_preview_apis defaults to true; set it to false if you do not accept preview APIs, which prevents deployment.

Set test_recipient to a mailbox approved to receive the three test reminders. Its default is null: deployment can prepare resources, but the source test will refuse to send carts until a recipient is configured. Do not put an action connection string, SQL password or customer mailing list in this file. Keep the schema name between 3 and 20 characters because it is the UDF connection alias.

Use Python 3.10+, Azure CLI, PowerShell on Windows and delegated access to an active supported Fabric capacity with SQL database creation enabled. The identity needs item creation and UDF execution permissions. The manual responses require the premium Data Activator and SQL Server connectors in Power Automate, an approved email connection, and Microsoft Entra ID access to the writable SQL database.

docs.title: 2. Deploy to Fabric
docs.text:
.\deploy.bat --config .\config.local.json --confirm-workspace $workspaceId

Open your workspace and find the schema, publishing function, Activator and CartFollowUp SQL database. Keep sql_destination.server and sql_destination.database from the command output for the SQL connection in Step 3. No carts have been sent yet; complete both response flows before running the sample.

The publisher inputs are customerId, customerEmail, cartId, cartValue, itemCount and lastActivityAt. Fabric rejects underscores in UDF parameter names; the original six event fields remain unchanged.

docs.title: 3. Complete manual setup before testing
docs.text:
1. Open the SQL database CartFollowUp, not its SQL analytics endpoint. In its SQL query editor, execute the package's setup.sql once, then record-cart-task.sql as a separate query. These create dbo.Customers, dbo.CartRecoveryTasks and dbo.RecordCartRecoveryTask. Confirm customers test-cart-a and test-cart-b and zero initial tasks. The scripts refuse existing tables instead of replacing data.
  2. Open CartActions, select the prepared Cart abandonment events event, and create Cart Recovery - Email and Cart Recovery - SQL Follow-up. Do not create another Activator or another Business Event source.
  3. Create a separate action named Send cart recovery reminder or Create cart follow-up task. Create each real custom action through Action → Type → New custom action, copy its own connection information, choose Open flow builder, authenticate the premium Data Activator connector and configure the matching trigger. The two actions need separate flows and their own connection information; never save signed connection information in configuration or shared evidence.

  4. The email flow uses the dynamic customer_email as recipient and includes cart_id and the six original fields. For the other flow, add SQL Server → Execute stored procedure, authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID, and select dbo.RecordCartRecoveryTask on the actual sql_destination.server and sql_destination.database. Use the same authorized database-owner identity for this exercise. If a separate connection identity is required, the database owner must grant it database access and EXECUTE on the procedure; independent reviewers need SELECT on both tables. Select each saved custom action in its rule, choose Edit action, and map the six fields below.

    Action input Event field Type customer_id customer_id String customer_email customer_email String cart_id cart_id String cart_value cart_value Number item_count item_count Number last_activity_at last_activity_at String

  5. In Execute stored procedure, bind the six trigger inputs to the same-named SQL parameters and bind the trigger's Activation ID (eventId) to activation_id. Do not compose SQL text from event values. The procedure returns the persisted task row; connector/procedure errors mean follow-up failed.

  6. For email, monitor cart_value with Is greater than 30 for each matching event. Do not use Becomes greater than, which can miss consecutive qualifying carts. For SQL follow-up, use On each value with no value filter. Save and activate both rules after checking the actual flow destinations.

Each registered customer can have several carts, but each cart has only one follow-up task. New tasks start as pending. A repeated delivery keeps the existing task, its status and creation time; conflicting cart details are reported as an error. Check the mailbox before retrying an uncertain email send, because the email connector can send a reminder more than once.

Check both saved flows and their destinations before sending the sample. Deployment leaves your manual action connections unchanged. Eventhouse history is an optional creation-time extension, not a requirement for this exercise.

docs.title: 4. Send carts and inspect recovery work
docs.text:
.\test.bat --config .\config.local.json --confirm-workspace $workspaceId

Run the sample once to send six abandoned carts for the two sample customers. The three carts above 30 should receive a reminder; all six should create a follow-up task. The supplied last-activity time is 45 minutes earlier to represent abandonment.

Sample cart Cart value Items Expected email Expected SQL task high-value 145.50 3 Yes Yes above-boundary 30.01 1 Yes Yes large-cart 250.00 5 Yes Yes boundary 30.00 2 No Yes below-boundary 29.99 1 No Yes zero-value 0.00 1 No Yes

docs.title: Evaluation criteria
docs.text:
1. Keep the six cart IDs returned by the sample. Use source_run_id to distinguish this exercise from earlier runs.
  2. In the approved mailbox, find three reminders with the qualifying cart IDs and match them to the email flow runs. Exact 30, 29.99 and 0 should have no reminder or email response.
  3. In dbo.CartRecoveryTasks, find six pending tasks and match them to the SQL flow runs. Check their task IDs, customer links and cart details.
  4. Compare each task with its sample cart: customer, email, value, item count and last-activity time should agree. Two carts belonging to the same customer must remain separate tasks.
  5. Allow at least five minutes for the responses. Check that the mailbox contains only the three qualifying reminders and the register contains six tasks.

This package does not measure checkout conversion, reward redemption or recovered revenue. Received-event history is an optional extension, not evidence that a reminder or task was completed.

Use the SQL query editor to inspect only the current run. Replace the placeholder with the actual source_run_id:

DECLARE @run_id uniqueidentifier = '<source_run_id>';
DECLARE @prefix nvarchar(42) = N'cicd-' + CONVERT(nvarchar(36), @run_id) + N'-';

SELECT t.task_id, t.cart_id, c.customer_id, c.display_name,
       t.customer_email, t.cart_value, t.item_count, t.last_activity_at,
       t.status, t.first_activation_id, t.created_at
FROM dbo.CartRecoveryTasks AS t
JOIN dbo.Customers AS c ON c.customer_id = t.customer_id
WHERE LEFT(t.cart_id, LEN(@prefix)) = @prefix
ORDER BY t.cart_id;

Compare the returned rows with the six sample carts, including their IDs and last-activity times. The task creation time is separate from the time the customer last used the cart. Values use single-precision numbers (float32, real in SQL), so minor display differences are expected; allow 1e-6 relative tolerance when comparing them and keep the strict above-30 reminder condition.

docs.title: Optional event history
docs.text:
The dashed branch in the business architecture is an extension, not another completion requirement. Choose Analyze in Eventhouse and its destination during Business Event creation if you are configuring an event natively with managed history. The package does not configure this association. Skip these queries for its deployed event; this Workbook does not provide a supported post-creation association procedure.

A source Eventhouse, a same-name table or a direct table write is not a managed Business Event subscription. History records received findings, not completed actions. Received-record counts can include repeated publications or deliveries and do not describe the full source population.

The following queries apply only to that creation-time history destination. Check delivered notifications or saved business outcomes separately. Keep currencies separate when comparing amounts.

History queries 
['Ecommerce.Cart.Abandoned']
| where ingestion_time() > ago(1h)

import datetime
import math
import re

import fabric.functions as fn

udf = fn.UserDataFunctions()


@udf.connection(argName="businessEventsClient", alias="EcommerceCart")
@udf.function()
def publish_cart_abandoned_event(
    businessEventsClient: fn.FabricBusinessEventsClient,
    customerId: str,
    customerEmail: str,
    cartId: str,
    cartValue: float,
    itemCount: int,
    lastActivityAt: str,
) -> dict:
    for value in (customerId, cartId):
        if not isinstance(value, str) or not value.strip() or value != value.strip() or len(value) > 128:
            raise ValueError("Customer and cart identifiers must be nonempty strings of at most 128 characters.")
    if (not isinstance(customerEmail, str) or len(customerEmail) > 254
            or not re.fullmatch(r"[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9-]+(?:\.[A-Za-z0-9-]+)+", customerEmail)):
        raise ValueError("Provide one valid customer email address without whitespace.")
    if type(cartValue) not in (int, float) or not math.isfinite(cartValue) or not 0 <= cartValue <= 1_000_000_000_000:
        raise ValueError("Cart value must be finite and nonnegative.")
    if type(itemCount) is not int or not 1 <= itemCount <= 2_147_483_647:
        raise ValueError("Item count must be a positive Avro int.")
    if not isinstance(lastActivityAt, str):
        raise ValueError("Last activity must be a timezone-aware UTC timestamp.")
    instant = datetime.datetime.fromisoformat(lastActivityAt.replace("Z", "+00:00"))
    if instant.tzinfo is None or instant.utcoffset() != datetime.timedelta(0):
        raise ValueError("Last activity must be a timezone-aware UTC timestamp.")
    businessEventsClient.PublishEvent(type="Ecommerce.Cart.Abandoned", event_data={
        "customer_id": customerId, "customer_email": customerEmail, "cart_id": cartId,
        "cart_value": float(cartValue), "item_count": itemCount, "last_activity_at": lastActivityAt,
    }, data_version="v1")
    return {"event_published": True}

docs.text: Use your configured names wherever they differ from the defaults.

docs.title: 3.1. Make the campaign catalog available
docs.text:
1. Open LoyaltyCatalogSetup, of type Notebook, in the deployed workspace.
  2. Attach LoyaltyCampaigns as its default Lakehouse and select Run all once.
  3. In LoyaltyCampaigns → Tables, open LoyaltyCampaignCatalog. Confirm the two rows: Gold at store-west has active campaign gold-west-welcome; Gold at store-east has inactive campaign gold-east-welcome. Both use benefit code GOLD_WELCOME.

docs.title: 3.2. Create the milestone publisher
docs.text:
Open the prepared LoyaltyQueries Queryset against LoyaltySource. The source table and both query tabs already exist; do not recreate them. Use your configured names wherever they differ from the defaults.

  1. If the query needs sample rows to expose its fields, run only the baseline block in Step 4. Do not run the increased balances yet.
  2. In Spend observations, select Set alert and create LoyaltyPublisher. In Activator, use observed_at as the event time and only customer_id as the object identity. Store, name, spend and timestamp are changing properties of that customer.
  3. Monitor total_spend. Choose Becomes greater than, or Increases above in the rule editor, with value 5000. Do not choose a condition that fires for every observation already above 5000.

  4. Configure Publish a business event, select RetailCustomers and Retail.Customer.MilestoneReached, and map:

    Event field Source property customer_id customer_id customer_name customer_name milestone_tier milestone_tier total_spend total_spend store_id store_id detected_at detected_at

See publishing Business Events from Activator.

docs.title: 3.3. Add campaign enrichment and Delta destinations
docs.text:
1. In Real-Time Hub, open Retail.Customer.MilestoneReached under RetailCustomers. Select Add consumer → Eventstream, use the same workspace, name it LoyaltyCampaignStream and select Connect. Use the native Business Event source, not a custom endpoint.
  2. Open the Eventstream in Edit mode. Add a reference source with Add source → Reference data sources → Select from OneLake. Choose LoyaltyCampaigns → Tables → LoyaltyCampaignCatalog, select all five catalog columns and save.

  3. Add a Join operation. Use the live Business Event stream on the left and the reference catalog on the right. Choose Left outer, with these two field pairs:

    Milestone field Catalog field milestone_tier catalog_tier store_id catalog_store_id

  4. From the joined stream, create the two branches below. Select the milestone's payload properties if a field picker shows them under data; do not use CloudEvents envelope fields. In Manage Fields, use the flat output column names shown below and check the resulting fields in preview before adding the destinations.

    Branch Filter Manage Fields: keep only Lakehouse table Campaign candidates campaign_id is not null and is_active equals boolean true customer_id, milestone_tier, total_spend, store_id, detected_at, campaign_id, benefit_code LoyaltyCampaignCandidates Campaign mapping review campaign_id is null customer_id, milestone_tier, total_spend, store_id, detected_at LoyaltyCampaignReview

  5. After each Manage Fields operation, select Add destination → Lakehouse, choose LoyaltyCampaigns, select JSON as the input data format and create the corresponding Delta table. For the small demonstration, use Minimum rows: 1 and Maximum duration: 1 minute. These settings favor visible sample results over efficient production-sized files.

  6. Publish the Eventstream. Confirm that the reference catalog is loaded and that both destination branches are running before starting the milestone exercise. Select a reference refresh schedule appropriate to later campaign changes; an edited catalog does not take effect until Eventstream refreshes it.

An inactive match is intentionally excluded from both outputs: it has a campaign mapping, but that campaign is not accepting candidates. An unmatched milestone goes to review so the team can decide whether to add a mapping. customer_name is not copied into either output because campaign preparation needs the customer ID, not another copy of their name.

This connection is manual because the public Eventstream definition API does not expose Business Events sources. See Eventstream transformations and Lakehouse destinations.

Then start the rule in LoyaltyPublisher. No consumer Activator, Power Automate flow or CRM connection is needed.

print customer_id = strcat(sample_id, '-eligible'), customer_name = 'Sample eligible',

docs.title: Evaluation criteria
docs.text:
Open LoyaltyCampaigns → SQL analytics endpoint. Allow time for Lakehouse ingestion and table visibility, then inspect the two Delta tables for this exercise:

SELECT customer_id, milestone_tier, total_spend, store_id,
       detected_at, campaign_id, benefit_code
FROM dbo.LoyaltyCampaignCandidates
WHERE customer_id LIKE 'loyalty-demo-001-%';

SELECT customer_id, milestone_tier, total_spend, store_id, detected_at
FROM dbo.LoyaltyCampaignReview
WHERE customer_id LIKE 'loyalty-demo-001-%';

Expect one distinct candidate customer, loyalty-demo-001-eligible, and one distinct review customer, loyalty-demo-001-unmatched. Both retain the gold, 5100, store and observation time from their milestone. No inactive, boundary or below-threshold customer belongs in the candidate table. Continued spending at 5200 should not create a new milestone or replace the original candidate.

The tables are append outputs, not an exactly-once audience or a reward ledger. Repeated deliveries can create duplicate rows; compare customer IDs and milestone context rather than treating every row as another customer. Before outreach, select one candidate per customer, tier and campaign, check contact permission and confirm benefit eligibility.

These records do not show reward issuance, membership updates, message delivery or improved retention.

docs.title: What you should see
docs.text:
Wait for the Notebook run to reach Completed, then check the responses and cases below.

The Workload values are case names, not statuses. For example, empty-completed and another-completed both produce status: "completed". The event statuses are failed, completed and skipped.

Workload Expected status Rows processed Expected SQL case failed-load failed 12 pending_triage failed-next-run failed 3 pending_triage completed completed 25 None: ignored empty-completed completed 0 None: ignored another-completed completed 8 None: ignored skipped skipped 0 None: ignored

Only the two failed outcomes match Register failed run. Expect two rule activations, two matching DataOpsFollowUp executions and two SQL cases initially marked pending_triage. Their rows_processed values are 12 and 3: each load failed after processing that many rows.

The three completed outcomes and the one skipped outcome are ignored by the Activator source filter, so they should not create responses or SQL cases. A successful workload that processes zero rows is still completed, not failed. Their absence from the follow-up table is expected: the queue contains only work that needs attention.

docs.title: Evaluation criteria
docs.text:
1. Confirm that the Notebook run reached Completed.
  2. In Register failed run and DataOpsFollowUp, expect two successful responses, one for each failure. Completed and skipped workloads should have no response.
  3. Open DataOpsCases, of type SQL database, and query dbo.PipelineFailureCases as shown below. Use the Notebook item ID returned as items.notebook by the test command. The table was empty before this test; expect exactly two rows for this Notebook.
  4. Check that both cases have status = "failed" and case_status = "pending_triage", with rows_processed values 12 and 3. Each case should retain its workload details and completion time. Both belong to the same Notebook, but their different run_id and case_id values identify two failures requiring separate follow-up.
  5. Observe the same run for at least five minutes without submitting it again. The table must remain at two cases, with no cases or response executions for completed or skipped.
SELECT case_id, pipeline_id, pipeline_name, run_id, status, rows_processed,

FROM dbo.PipelineFailureCases
WHERE pipeline_id = N'<source-notebook-item-id>'
ORDER BY created_at, run_id;

The two cases are ready for triage. The test does not retry the failed loads or repair their data.

        raise RuntimeError("The workload outcome was not accepted for publication.")
    print(event)


def execute_workload(work, run_id):
    progress = {"rows_processed": 0}
    started = time.monotonic()
    status = "completed"
    try:
        work(progress)
    except SkippedWorkload:
        status = "skipped"
        logging.info("Workload %s was explicitly skipped.", run_id)
    except Exception:
        status = "failed"
        logging.exception("Workload %s failed.", run_id)
        raise
    finally:
        publish_outcome(validate_event({
            "pipeline_id": PIPELINE_ID,
            "pipeline_name": PIPELINE_NAME,
            "run_id": run_id,
            "status": status,
            "rows_processed": progress["rows_processed"],
            "duration_seconds": int(time.monotonic() - started),
            "triggered_by": "manual",
            "completed_at": datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc).isoformat().replace("+00:00", "Z"),
        }))

import datetime
import uuid
import fabric.functions as fn

udf = fn.UserDataFunctions()


@udf.connection(argName="caseDatabase", alias="FailureCases")
@udf.function()
def register_pipeline_failure(
    caseDatabase: fn.FabricSqlConnection,
    pipelineId: str, pipelineName: str, runId: str, status: str,
    rowsProcessed: int, durationSeconds: int, triggeredBy: str, completedAt: str,
) -> dict:
    event = validate_event({
        "pipeline_id": pipelineId, "pipeline_name": pipelineName, "run_id": runId,
        "status": status, "rows_processed": rowsProcessed, "duration_seconds": durationSeconds,
        "triggered_by": triggeredBy, "completed_at": completedAt,
    })
    if status != "failed":
        raise ValueError("Only failed executions may reach case registration.")
    connection = caseDatabase.connect()
    try:
        connection.autocommit = True
        cursor = connection.cursor()
        cursor.execute(
            "EXEC dbo.RecordPipelineFailure @pipeline_id=?, @pipeline_name=?, @run_id=?, @status=?, "
            "@rows_processed=?, @duration_seconds=?, @triggered_by=?, @completed_at=?",
            *[event[name] for name in FIELDS],
        )
        row = cursor.fetchone()
        if row is None:
            raise RuntimeError("Case registration returned no persisted row.")
        result = dict(zip([column[0] for column in cursor.description], row))
        if (any(type(result.get(name)) is not type(value) or result[name] != value for name, value in event.items())
                or result.get("case_status") not in ("pending_triage", "in_progress", "resolved")):
            raise RuntimeError("The persisted case does not match the failed execution.")
        result["case_id"] = str(uuid.UUID(str(result["case_id"])))
        created = result["created_at"]
        if not isinstance(created, datetime.datetime) or created.tzinfo is not None:
            raise RuntimeError("SQL did not return the expected UTC datetime2 creation time.")
        result["created_at"] = created.replace(tzinfo=datetime.timezone.utc).isoformat().replace("+00:00", "Z")
        return result
    finally:
        connection.close()

import datetime
import math
import fabric.functions as fn

udf = fn.UserDataFunctions()

def required_text(value, name, maximum):
    if not isinstance(value, str) or not value.strip():
        raise ValueError(f"{name} must be a non-empty string")
    value = value.strip()
    if len(value) > maximum:
        raise ValueError(f"{name} must be at most {maximum} characters")
    return value

@udf.connection(argName="businessEventsClient", alias="OrderRiskSchema")
@udf.function()
def evaluate_order_risk(
    businessEventsClient: fn.FabricBusinessEventsClient,
    orderId: str,
    customerId: str,
    riskScore: float,
    decidedAt: str,
) -> dict:
    orderId = required_text(orderId, "orderId", 128)
    customerId = required_text(customerId, "customerId", 128)
    if isinstance(riskScore, bool) or not isinstance(riskScore, (int, float)):
        raise ValueError("riskScore must be a number")
    if not math.isfinite(riskScore) or not 0 <= riskScore <= 1:
        raise ValueError("riskScore must be finite and between 0 and 1")
    decidedAt = required_text(decidedAt, "decidedAt", 64)
    instant = datetime.datetime.fromisoformat(decidedAt.replace("Z", "+00:00"))
    if instant.tzinfo is None or instant.utcoffset() != datetime.timedelta(0):
        raise ValueError("decidedAt must use timezone-aware UTC")
    decision = (
        "hold" if riskScore >= 0.85
        else "manual_review" if riskScore >= 0.55
        else "release"
    )
    businessEventsClient.PublishEvent(
        type="Ecommerce.Order.FraudDecision",
        event_data={
            "order_id": orderId,
            "customer_id": customerId,
            "risk_score": float(riskScore),
            "decision": decision,
            "decided_at": instant.isoformat().replace("+00:00", "Z"),
        },
        data_version="v1",
    )
    return {"decision": decision, "event_published": True}

import fabric.functions as fn
import logging

udf = fn.UserDataFunctions()

# The alias must match the connection configured in Manage connections
@udf.connection(argName='businessEventsClient', alias='RetailInventory')

def publish_low_stock_event(

    productId: str,
    productName: str,
    storeId: str,
    currentStock: int,
    threshold: int,
    supplierId: str,

docs.title: Order History Analysis: Workbook
docs.text:
Business context and architecture

Publish six synthetic orders, retain the received events in Eventhouse and compare order volume and value across two stores. This Beginner exercise uses guided native setup and one KQL result check. It has no downloadable deployment package.

Use an isolated learning workspace and unused item names. If these names already exist, choose new names and change eventSchemaSet in the source cell accordingly. Do not replace an existing event or its history configuration.

docs.text:
Use a Fabric workspace on an active supported capacity with permission to create Business Events, an Eventhouse and a Notebook. The Notebook needs a supported Fabric runtime with Python 3.12+ and Business Events support.

Publish permission on the Event Schema Set and permission to query the history database are required. If a separate owner manages the schema set, have that owner grant the appropriate data access role before publishing. See Publish Business Events.

All records are generated in the Notebook. No tenant IDs, saved credentials, production endpoints or real order data are supplied by this Workbook.

docs.text:
1. In Fabric, open Real-Time hub → Business events → New business event → Create new schema.
  2. Select your learning workspace and create the Event Schema Set OrderHistorySchema. Name the event Retail.Orders.OrderPlaced and use schema version v1.
  3. Define these payload fields. The JSON below is the corresponding Avro schema reference, not a second setup route.
Field Type Meaning sample_run_id string Correlates one execution of this exercise order_id string Identifies one synthetic order store_id string north or south order_total_usd double Placed-order value in USD placed_at string UTC placement time in ISO 8601 format

  "type": "record",
  "name": "OrderPlaced",

  "fields": [
    {"name": "sample_run_id", "type": "string"},

docs.title: 2. Publish one sample
docs.text:
Create OrderHistoryPublisher in the same workspace. Replace <workspace-name-or-id> below with your workspace name or ID, then run this Python cell.

from datetime import datetime, timezone
from uuid import uuid4

import notebookutils

sample_run_id = str(uuid4())
placed_at = datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()
orders = [
    ("north", 120.0),
    ("north", 80.0),
    ("north", 150.0),
    ("south", 200.0),
    ("south", 50.0),
    ("south", 300.0),
]
events = [
    {
        "sample_run_id": sample_run_id,
        "order_id": f"{sample_run_id}-{index:02d}",
        "store_id": store_id,
        "order_total_usd": amount,
        "placed_at": placed_at,
    }
    for index, (store_id, amount) in enumerate(orders, start=1)
]

published = notebookutils.businessEvents.publish(
    eventSchemaSetWorkspace="<workspace-name-or-id>",
    eventSchemaSet="OrderHistorySchema",
    eventTypeName="Retail.Orders.OrderPlaced",
    eventData=events,
    dataVersion="v1",
)
if published is not True:
    raise RuntimeError("Publication was not accepted. Inspect the Notebook error before retrying.")

print(f"Sample run: {sample_run_id}")
print("Publication accepted. Verify receipt and totals in Eventhouse next.")

Copy the printed Sample run value. Each execution creates a new run identifier; use the identifier from the execution you want to inspect. Publication success does not prove delivery to Eventhouse.

docs.title: 3. Compare stores in KQL
docs.text:
In the event-history database, open a KQL query. Replace <event-history-table> with the table actually created in step 1 and <sample-run-id> with the printed identifier.

The query accepts a table with payload fields exposed as columns or a CloudEvents data column. It filters the run before deduplicating by order identifier, so prior exercises and repeated delivery do not inflate this comparison.

let SampleRun = "<sample-run-id>";
['<event-history-table>']
| extend payload = parse_json(tostring(column_ifexists("data", pack_all())))
| extend sample_run_id = tostring(payload.sample_run_id),
         order_id = tostring(payload.order_id),
         store_id = tostring(payload.store_id),
         order_total_usd = todouble(payload.order_total_usd),
         placed_at = todatetime(payload.placed_at)
| where sample_run_id == SampleRun
| summarize arg_max(placed_at, store_id, order_total_usd) by order_id
| summarize Orders = count(), OrderValueUSD = sum(order_total_usd) by store_id
| order by store_id asc

docs.title: Expected result
docs.text:
store_id Orders OrderValueUSD north 3 350 south 3 550

The two rows represent six distinct orders and USD 900 in placed-order value. Completion means these results are visible for the same run that the Notebook printed, not just that the publication call returned successfully.

If no rows appear, allow time for ingestion and rerun the query, not the publisher. Check the actual database, table, sample identifier, schema version and creation-time history choice. Inspect a received row to confirm its payload shape if fields are missing; do not treat an empty result or missing field as zero business activity.

docs.title: What this exercise demonstrates
docs.text:
A Business Event can feed an independent, queryable history without coupling the publisher to an analytics table. Here, managed Eventhouse history is the required consumer. In the operational scenarios it is an optional additional consumer instead.

The sample query deduplicates only this exercise's order identifiers. It does not reconcile changing orders, payments, cancellations or refunds. Keep production retention, access controls and reconciliation rules separate from this synthetic exercise.

Run the sample once to represent six viewer interactions. The two watches and one like should each produce a recommendation list; the click, search and skip should not. Use the viewer and session IDs returned by the sample to find the results.

Interaction Content Expected recommendations, in order watch space-explorer mars-mission, robot-future, ocean-depths like city-mystery case-notes, hidden-case, quiet-city watch quiet-city family-roads, case-notes, hidden-case click space-explorer No response search space-explorer No response skip city-mystery No response

The first two interactions belong to the same viewer and session. The like has an earlier timestamp: both lists should remain available rather than one replacing the other.

docs.title: Evaluation criteria
docs.text:
1. Keep the viewer and session IDs returned by the sample, using source_run_id to distinguish this exercise from earlier runs.
  2. In Refresh session recommendations and ViewerRefresh, check that the two watches and one like each received a successful response.
  3. Open ViewerRecommendations → Files → ViewerRecommendations. Expect three <recommendation_id>.json files with status: "ready_for_serving". Match their viewer, session, action and time to the sample, and compare the suggested content and its order with the table.
  4. Confirm no response execution or file for click, search or skip. Event delivery is asynchronous; inspect the run over at least five minutes, not just the first file.
  5. Confirm the shared session retains both different recommendation lists. The interacted content must never appear among its own recommendations.

Each file also records the ranking method, catalog identity/hash, rule and creation time for later review. An identical interaction keeps its original list and timestamp; different interactions remain separate. Changed results for the same interaction are reported as an error rather than replacing an existing list.

The exercise finishes with three saved recommendation lists and no lists for excluded actions. Displaying them in an application and measuring engagement are separate next steps.

import datetime
import fabric.functions as fn

udf = fn.UserDataFunctions()


@udf.connection(argName="businessEventsClient", alias="ViewerSchema")
@udf.function()
def publish_viewer_behavior_event(
    businessEventsClient: fn.FabricBusinessEventsClient,
    viewerId: str,
    sessionId: str,
    contentId: str,
    action: str,
    occurredAt: str,
) -> dict:
    event = {
        "viewer_id": viewerId, "session_id": sessionId, "content_id": contentId,
        "action": action, "occurred_at": occurredAt,
    }
    if any(not isinstance(value, str) or not value.strip() or len(value) > 128 for value in event.values()):

    if action not in ("click", "search", "watch", "skip", "like"):
        raise ValueError("Use a supported lowercase interaction.")
    if datetime.datetime.fromisoformat(occurredAt.replace("Z", "+00:00")).utcoffset() != datetime.timedelta(0):
        raise ValueError("Use a timezone-aware UTC timestamp.")
    businessEventsClient.PublishEvent(
        type="Streaming.Viewer.BehaviorDetected", event_data=event, data_version="v1",
    )

1. Open Microsoft Fabric.
  2. In the left navigation, select Workspaces, then open the workspace used in your configuration.
  3. Open RevenueQueries, of type KQL Queryset. Confirm that its data source is RevenueSource, the KQL database in RevenueData.

  2. Under Files, open RevenueInvestigations. This folder is empty before the first real event-driven investigation.
  3. Return to the workspace and open RevenueInvestigation, of type Data pipeline. Its notebook activity targets RevenueInvestigationNotebook.
  4. Select that activity and inspect its Settings and base parameters. The six event fields come from corresponding pipeline parameters; pipeline_run_id comes from @pipeline().RunId, not a supplied event field or a static value.
  5. Open RevenueActions, of type Activator, and inspect Prepare revenue investigation. It uses On each value, with a Data Pipeline action targeting RevenueInvestigation and dynamic mappings for all six original event fields.

docs.text:
RevenuePublisher contains the native KQL connection, the Revenue reporting period object and the stopped Revenue below target rule. The deployment has already configured its condition, Business Event destination and six dynamic mappings. Do not create another alert from the Queryset or Dashboard when using this package.

  1. Return to the workspace and open the existing RevenuePublisher item, of type Activator, not RevenueActions.
  2. Switch Activator to Edit. Keep the baseline from section 3.1: revenue 90000, target 100000, variance -10.

  3. In the left Explorer, expand Revenue native source contract → Revenue reporting period and select Revenue below target, identified by a lightning-bolt icon.

    Select the rule, not Revenue native source event, Revenue period observations or the variance_pct property. Selecting a source event shows Live feed, not the rule editor. Selecting the rule opens its Definition pane and rule controls.

  4. Confirm that the rule is stopped: Start is enabled and Stop is disabled. If it is running, select Stop before continuing.

  5. In Definition, check Attribute: variance_pct, Condition: Decreases below and Value: -15, not -0.15. Some editor layouts label the same crossing condition Becomes → Less than → -15. Occurrence is Every time the condition is met.
  6. In Definition → Action, confirm Publish a business event, with Sales.Revenue.BelowTarget in RevenueSchema.

  7. Select View action to open Edit the action. If the button is labeled Edit action, select that instead. Inspect the six preconfigured dynamic mappings without replacing them:

    Event field Source value region region period_start period_start revenue revenue target target variance_pct variance_pct detected_at detected_at

    Do not use fixed sample values or parse the combined Composite key to fill the event.

  8. Close the action editor without changing the mappings, using its top-right Close (X) button, not Apply. Leave the publication rule stopped until section 3.4.

See creating Activator rules and properties and Activator Business Event publishing.

Keep the reporting period consistent. The Composite key identifies the region and reporting period as a two-value array; changing revenue must not create a new monitored period. While the rule is stopped, open Revenue period observations and append a fresh baseline. docs.text:
1. Check the publication rule, six field mappings and region-period key before starting the monitor.
  2. Open the publication rule in RevenuePublisher and select Start.
  3. Append a fresh 90000/100000 snapshot. Wait until Revenue period observations shows the new timestamp and -10 baseline before continuing.

RevenueActions is already enabled and bound to RevenueInvestigation. Do not start the pipeline manually.

docs.title: 4. Test the flow from KQL
docs.text:
Start with the monitor ready and the region-period key checked. The exercise follows one reporting period as revenue falls below target, recovers and falls again.

  1. With RevenuePublisher running, check that Revenue period observations shows revenue 90000, target 100000 and variance -10.
  2. Return to RevenueQueries and run the snapshot command from section 3.1 for each state below, editing only revenue. Keep target 100000, region West and period 2026-11-01.
  3. Add each snapshot separately with observed_at = now(). Wait until Activator shows that state before moving to the next row. Keep all snapshots and the unfiltered monitoring query so recovery and repeated shortfalls can be distinguished. A Dashboard refresh or waiting a fixed time is not a substitute for checking Activator.

Follow this sequence in order:

Source state Revenue Variance Expected new Business Event / pipeline execution Baseline 90000 -10 None Exact boundary 85000 -15 None First crossing below 80000 -20 One Remaining below 78000 -22 None Recovery above 90000 -10 None Second crossing below 80000 -20 One

Each crossing should publish Sales.Revenue.BelowTarget and automatically prepare an investigation. Allow time for monitoring, delivery and Spark startup. Leave the pipeline to start from the event rather than running it manually.

docs.title: Evaluation criteria
docs.text:
For each crossing, check the investigation before continuing, using the checks below:

  • Only the two crossings below -15 should create events and start the pipeline. The exact boundary and a further decline while already below target should not create another investigation.
  • Open RevenueInvestigations → Files → RevenueInvestigations. Expect two new JSON analyses with status ready_for_review, each linked by pipeline_run_id to its completed pipeline run. Check the six event values and UTC investigated_at. For 80000/100000, the analysis should show variance -20%, shortfall 20000 and required lift 25%.
  • Each analysis describes the revenue position that triggered it. A retry within the same pipeline run keeps the existing file; a separate pipeline run has its own file, so count incidents by the source events as well as saved files.
  • Finally, try zero and negative targets. Expect KQL null variance and no event or pipeline response during two observed active source polls. These are invalid targets, not revenue shortfalls requiring investigation.

The outcome is analysis ready for the revenue team's review. It is not an approved recovery plan or evidence that revenue has recovered.

    'store_id': store_id,
    'expected_transactions': expected,
    'actual_transactions': actual,
    'deviation_pct': deviation_pct,
    'window_start': "2024-06-22T09:00:00Z",
    'severity': severity
}

# Publish to Business Events
notebookutils.businessEvents.publish(
    eventSchemaSetWorkspace=WORKSPACE_NAME,
    eventSchemaSet=SCHEMA_SET_NAME,
    eventTypeName=EVENT_NAME,
    eventData=payload,
    dataVersion='v1'
)
